title: Auditor review process inconsistent, unclear
full_text:
The nation’s three accounting bodies have called for greater clarity and consistency in how the ATO conducts its reviews of SMSF auditors while recognising the professional judgment they bring to their work.
Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand, CPA Australia and the Institute of Public Accountants made the comment in a joint submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s performance audit of the ATO’s regulation of SMSFs.
While stating they believe the SMSF sector to be generally well run and regulated, member feedback across the three bodies raised concerns about the length of the auditor review processes, as well as inconsistent service experiences and communication difficulties for practitioners dealing with the regulator.
“Member feedback indicates that ATO reviews can involve lengthy timeframes, requests for additional information well after initial contact and insufficient clarity about the scope and focus of the review. Members also report further delays where an auditor disputes a preliminary finding,” the submission stated.
“We suggest the ATO consider clear service-level commitments for the key stages of an auditor review. These could include a defined scope at the outset, expected timeframes and a clear path to escalate or seek review of findings.
“We would also encourage the ATO to establish appropriate key performance indicators and outcome metrics, supported by regular public reporting, to assess the effectiveness of its reviews and their contribution to improving audit quality.”
The joint bodies added the issue of consistency was also reflected in the service received by auditors and the application of standards by ATO staff, with their members reporting variations in the regulator’s approach to auditor reviews, including the technical expertise applied and the clarity of communication.
“These variations can create uncertainty about how the ATO assesses compliance with the standards. We recommend consistent review processes supported by reviewers with practical audit experience to strengthen confidence in the review process,” the submission noted.
“We are concerned by the ATO’s tendency to adopt bright-line interpretations of principles-based auditing standards that require professional judgment, including in relation to auditor independence, audit evidence and documentation.
“This can, in effect, create a quasi-standard-setting or interpretation role, with regulatory expectations treated as prescriptive requirements rather than allowing for the exercise of judgment within the standards.
“While we recognise the practical reasons for seeking clear and consistent expectations, we consider that standard setting and authoritative interpretation should remain independent of regulation and oversight.
“We therefore recommend that the ATO address relevant issues through engagement with the responsible standard setters and the audit community, rather than through unilateral interpretations that effectively supplement or narrow the standards.”
